implementation_notes: There is no standard-library persistence context, so the accumulator is a dirty map keyed by row id and the flusher is a dedicated thread. Stage under a std::mutex and wake the flusher through a std::condition_variable; on C++20 use std::jthread, whose stop_token and joining destructor make the flusher's lifetime exception-safe, and pre-C++20 use std::thread with an explicit stop flag. The drained batch is executed in one transaction over prepared statements; what replaces the classic structure is only the thread and synchronization primitives, so the roles stay hand-written and are justified when write throughput matters.
pitfalls: Use the predicated wait (or re-check after every wake-up): condition variables wake spuriously and a naive wait flushes an empty batch or misses the wake-up.
Destroying the flusher without draining loses staged writes - jthread joins but does not flush, so the destructor must drain explicitly.
Staging by copying whole rows under the lock serializes producers: stage a move-constructed snapshot and keep the critical section minimal.
